trends: U.S. offshore balancing and allied self-reliance

As the United States hands primary responsibility for defense to its allies, self-strengthening is under way on several fronts at once: Japan's normalization of its defense posture, Europe's rearmament, and the Mecca pact among Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. A by-product is mounting pressure toward nuclear proliferation. Conditions are forming for debates over independent nuclear capabilities to grow in South Korea, Japan, and Saudi Arabia.

Cooperation among Russia, North Korea, and Iran has tied Ukraine, the Middle East, and the Korean Peninsula together. How the war on one front ends changes each country's calculations on the others. Once the Russia-Ukraine war ends, North Korea will be of less use to Russia, and Pyongyang will have more incentive to turn toward the United States and China.

India, Turkey, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Saudi Arabia join neither camp, lining up issue by issue. Small arrangements such as the Mecca pact, the Quad, and AUKUS, rather than grand alliances, are moving the board.

The Hormuz blockade is forcing Asian importers to diversify their crude oil supply routes. The Strait of Malacca gains weight, India's and China's dependence on Russian oil deepens, and Saudi Arabia's bypass pipelines become both strategic assets and targets.

Technological self-reliance and military modernization put time on China's side, but slowing growth, a shrinking population, and military purges work in the opposite direction. The most dangerous moment will come when China concludes that the time working in its favor is running out.
AI concentrates value in a few hubs and turns those hubs into targets

AI cannot escape geography. Leading-edge chipmaking is concentrated in Taiwan and helium production in the United States and Qatar, and as the 2026 attacks on data centers in the Gulf and in Kyiv showed, such hubs become targets. The more these choke points are threatened, the faster rerouting and dispersal proceed, with the exception of irreplaceable choke points such as Hormuz.

thinkers.claim: He divided the causes of the war into the reasons openly given and what he called the truest cause. The disputes over Corcyra and Potidaea were the reasons given; the truest cause was the growth of Athenian power and the fear it aroused in Sparta (1.23.6). This is why he is called the founder of realism. Yet the maxim that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must belongs to the Athenian envoys who demanded the surrender of Melos in 416 BCE; it is not his own conclusion (5.89). Directly after his account of the execution of the adult men of Melos and the sale of its women and children into slavery (5.116), he narrates how Athens was crushed in the Sicilian expedition (415–413 BCE). He also wrote that after the plague neither fear of the gods nor law held anyone back (2.53), and that war is a rough teacher that brings people's characters down to the level of their circumstances (3.82). He recorded the damage war does even to individual health and to the community.
thinkers.now: The Allison entry in the list of reference thinkers interprets the reciprocal visits of the U.S. and Chinese leaders in 2026 and the tariff truce extended to January 2027 as efforts to manage the relationship so as to avoid the Thucydides Trap. In Thucydides's terms, tariffs and arms sales to Taiwan are the reasons given; the shift in power and the fear beneath them do not disappear with a summit. Clisa Geopolitics places a commitment formalizing South Korean military participation in a Taiwan contingency at the bottom of its ranking, citing in support the case of Athens, which made only a defensive alliance with Corcyra yet was drawn into the fighting anyway (1.44–55). In the Russia-Ukraine war, the Easter, Victory Day, and early-September ceasefires all ended in renewed fighting, and the site, pointing to the Peace of Nicias, judges that a ceasefire without guarantees, an outcome it puts at 17 percent, may be only one phase of a war of attrition.
thinkers.record: Where he has been borne out: a Harvard Belfer Center case study that generalizes his diagnosis of the Peloponnesian War in 1.23.6, made in the late fifth century BCE, found that 12 of the 16 cases since the late 15th century in which a rising power confronted an established one ended in war. His observation that those who survived the plague of 430 BCE either did not catch it again or did not die if they did (2.51.6) is regarded as an early record of acquired immunity. Where he has fallen short: in the same study, four cases, including the United States and the Soviet Union during the Cold War and the United Kingdom and France with Germany from the 1990s onward, passed without war. As for the Peloponnesian War itself, Kagan in 1969 saw it as an avoidable war, and Wang pointed out in 2020 that the side that opened it was the established power. These criticisms converge on the view that shifts in power and fear create the conditions for war, while whether war actually begins depends on leaders' choices.

thinkers.claim: In the Republic, Socrates says that the ills of cities will not cease unless philosophers become kings or kings take up philosophy. This is the archetype of the question of rule by expertise. Books 8 and 9 explain how the best city decays in turn into timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny. Change begins with division within the ruling group (545d); excessive freedom turns into excessive servitude and gives rise to tyranny (564a); and the tyrant keeps stirring up wars so that the people will need a leader (566e) and holds on to power only by getting rid of the brave and the wise (567b–c). In Book 1 of the Laws, it is the Cretan Clinias who says that peace is only a name, and the Athenian who leads the dialogue counters that legislation should aim at peace, not war. Plato set the happiness of the whole city, not of a single class (420b), as the purpose of politics; in that respect his starting point differs from that of Clisa Geopolitics, which takes the capabilities of individual human beings as its purpose.
thinkers.now: The Power Structures tab of Clisa Geopolitics describes North Korea as a system of one-man rule by the general secretary, who is also chairman of the State Affairs Commission, and Russia as a system in which authority is concentrated in the president. In Iran, Mojtaba Khamenei succeeded his late father as supreme leader in March 2026, and in China, the purges of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli left only two of the seven members of the Central Military Commission in place, concentrating decision-making even further in the hands of President Xi Jinping. In countries like these, war and negotiation hinge on the judgment of a few. In the Republic, Plato hoped that such judgment would be wise; in the Laws, he distrusted unchecked rulers and chose law.
thinkers.record: Where he has fallen short: his visits to Syracuse around 366 and around 361 BCE, which put rule by philosophers to the test, failed. According to the Seventh Letter, he went to teach Dionysius II for fear of seeming a man of mere words, but Dion was driven into exile by slander, and Plato himself barely got away on his third visit. Dion later seized power and was assassinated. Against the scheme in which regimes degenerate in a fixed order, Aristotle cited counterexamples in Book 5, Chapter 12 of the Politics, in which oligarchy turned into tyranny and one tyranny into another. Where he has been borne out: the proposition in Republic 545d, that a regime does not change as long as its ruling group holds together, points in the same direction as the 1986 conclusion of Guillermo O'Donnell and Philippe Schmitter that no transition has begun without important divisions within the regime itself. Barbara Geddes, however, argued in 2004 that splits lead to collapse mainly in military regimes, and that in one-man dictatorships, which suppress factions, splits become dangerous only when compounded by events such as the leader's serious illness.

thinkers.claim: Book 1, Chapter 7 of the Nicomachean Ethics defines the human good (happiness, or eudaimonia) as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, carried on over a complete life (1098a16–18). Happiness, in other words, is not a feeling but a life lived exercising one's capacities well. The Politics holds that the state (polis) exists for the sake of living well and is not merely an alliance to prevent injustice (Book 3, Chapter 9). It distinguishes kingship, aristocracy, and polity from their corrupt forms of tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy, according to whether one, a few, or many rule, and whether they rule for the common interest or for themselves (Book 3, Chapter 7). He held that a state with a large middle class is likely to be well governed (Book 4, Chapter 11) and that inequality is everywhere the cause of revolution (Book 5). In her 1988 paper "Nature, Function, and Capability," Martha Nussbaum argued that Amartya Sen is at one with Aristotle in valuing goods by the human functioning they make possible, and she built the capabilities approach on Aristotle.
thinkers.now: Clisa Geopolitics takes the happiness of individual human beings as its final end but does not define happiness itself; instead, it measures capabilities, the conditions for pursuing the life each person considers good, across the seven categories of human security defined by the UN. Unlike Aristotle, who also laid out what a good life consists of, it measures only the conditions. Clisa Geopolitics also distinguishes regime survival from people's lives, which follows the same line as his distinction between rule for the common interest and rule for the ruler's own sake. On Iran, too, it sums up the Iranian government's yardstick as regime survival, while recommending, from the standpoint of individual lives, that humanitarian aid for the Iranian people be raised through diplomatic channels as well.
thinkers.record: Where he has been borne out: Seymour Martin Lipset, acknowledging Aristotle's influence, argued in 1959 that a middle class enlarged by economic development sustains democracy, in line with the proposition in Book 4, Chapter 11 of the Politics that a country with a large middle class is likely to be well governed; and Adam Przeworski and Fernando Limongi showed in 1997, using data on 135 countries from 1950 to 1990, that the richer a country, the more stable its democracy. Where he has fallen short: in the same study, economic development did not raise the probability of a transition to democracy, and Andrew Nathan reported in 2016 that China's middle class supports the authoritarian regime even as it embraces liberal values. His thinking on the size of the state also missed the mark. Though he tutored Alexander, he theorized only the polis, and after his death in 322 BCE most Greek poleis lost any real independence under the successor kingdoms.

thinkers.role: Philosopher, professor at the University of Königsberg
thinkers.claim: Of the six preliminary articles in Toward Perpetual Peace, Kant classed three as laws to be observed immediately: the first, that a peace treaty concluded with a secret reservation of grounds for a future war is merely a truce; the fifth, that no state should forcibly interfere in the constitution and government of another; and the sixth, which forbids, even in wartime, hostilities that would make mutual trust impossible in a future peace. The three definitive articles are a republican constitution, a federation of free states, and a cosmopolitan right limited to universal hospitality. By a republic he meant not democracy but a system that separates legislative from executive power. The federation is not a world state but a league of peace without coercive power, what he called a negative surrogate, offered because states reject a world republic. Cosmopolitan right is a right to visit, not a right to take possession, and in the same passage he condemned European colonial conquest. Underlying all of this is the categorical imperative to treat people never merely as means but always at the same time as ends, a formulation also quoted in the philosophy questions section of Clisa Geopolitics.
thinkers.now: On the Korean Peninsula, Clisa Geopolitics invokes the sixth preliminary article in judging that information operations aimed at North Korea that come close to inciting regime overthrow are something Seoul should restrain on its own rather than hold in reserve as a bargaining chip. In the Russia-Ukraine war, the short ceasefires at Easter, on Victory Day, and in early September all ended in renewed fighting, and Clisa Geopolitics puts the probability of a Minsk-style ceasefire without guarantees from great-power troops at 17 percent. This is the same diagnosis as the first article: a treaty that leaves the seeds of a future war is merely a truce. Under a literal reading of the fifth article, the U.S. military's capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January amounts to prohibited forcible interference. On the Taiwan Strait, the finding that Congress has offset or delayed the U.S. administration's deals with China through the Taiwan Relations Act and other means echoes Kant's view of the separation of powers as the core of a republic. NATO, a party to the Russia-NATO standoff, is a collective defense alliance against external threats, so its purpose differs from that of Kant's league of peace, which aims to end war among its own members.
thinkers.record: Where he has been borne out: on Kant's 1795 view that republics would hesitate to go to war, Michael Doyle reported in Philosophy & Public Affairs in 1983 that constitutionally secure liberal states had not fought one another for almost 200 years, and explained this through Kant's three definitive articles. John Oneal and Bruce Russett, using data from 1885 to 1992, reported that democracy, economic interdependence, and membership in international organizations lower the likelihood of armed conflict (Triangulating Peace, 2001). Where he has fallen short: Doyle himself noted that liberal states are not peaceful toward nonliberal ones, pointing out that the advance to the Yalu River in the Korean War and the Vietnam War instead deepened the adversaries' dependence on the Soviet Union. Among the covert interventions he left out of his analysis, those aimed at elected governments, such as Árbenz's in Guatemala and Allende's in Chile, point to a remaining problem: democratic peace theory looks only at open war. Whether to treat the 1999 Kargil conflict between India and Pakistan as an exception also depends on how democracy is defined.

thinkers.claim: In a lecture to the Royal Geographical Society on January 25, 1904, Mackinder argued that the "Columbian epoch," the 400 years in which a sea-dominant Western Europe had encircled Eurasia from outside, had ended around 1900. The pivot region is the interior of Eurasia, inaccessible to ships but open in earlier ages to mounted nomads. What he saw first in the railway was military mobility. A state at the center of the continent that moved troops and supplies by rail along short internal routes could concentrate its strength ahead of a sea power that had to take the long way around by sea, a logic known as the advantage of interior lines. His evidence was the Russian railway running 6,000 miles from the western frontier to Vladivostok and the Russian army in Manchuria. His warning was that if this pivot state expanded to the margins of Eurasia and used the continent's resources to build a fleet, world empire would be within sight, and he named an alliance between Germany and Russia as the event that could set this in motion.
thinkers.now: The Russia-Ukraine war is a fight over what Mackinder called Eastern Europe: the western gateway into the Heartland. Continued attrition is rated the most likely future through 2030, at 36 percent. A war of attrition now in its fifth year shows that even a Heartland state cannot easily take control of Eastern Europe. In 1919, Mackinder described the Baltic as, strategically, a closed sea of the Heartland, but since Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024) joined NATO, the Baltic has become a sea ringed mostly by NATO members. Over Kaliningrad, the Russian territory on its shores, Russia warned NATO on September 30 that if the exclave were blockaded, it could use all weapons, including nuclear weapons.
thinkers.record: The German-Russian alliance that he named in 1904 as the event that could lead to world empire came closest to reality with the German-Soviet Nonaggression Pact of August 1939, but it did not last two years: Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941. His 1919 proposition that whoever rules East Europe commands the Heartland seemed to hold when the Soviet Union, having taken control of Eastern Europe after World War II, became a superpower facing the United States, but the Soviet Union, too, dissolved in December 1991 without ever ruling the World-Island. The North Atlantic framework he proposed in 1943 became reality six years later with the founding of NATO in April 1949, but the Soviet Union, which he had meant to include, became the adversary NATO was built to contain. The tier of buffer states in Eastern Europe that he prescribed in 1919, by contrast, collapsed with the German and Soviet invasions of Poland in September 1939. The interior's advantage, which he traced in 1904 to its inaccessibility to ships, diminished sharply with the arrival of aircraft, missiles, and nuclear weapons, as Amery had anticipated that same year.

thinkers.role: American scholar of international politics, professor at Yale University
thinkers.claim: Spykman accepted Mackinder's map but reversed his conclusion. Because the Heartland has little arable land and is ringed by ice and high mountains that make transport difficult, he reasoned that Soviet power would remain west of the Urals unless the resources of Central Asia proved comparable to those of the rimland. The decisive zone was the rimland, the belt between the Heartland and the surrounding seas that runs from the European coastland through Arabia and the Middle East to the monsoon lands of India and East Asia. The rimland was an amphibious zone that had to defend itself on both land and sea, and a vast buffer zone where land power and sea power collided. The core of U.S. security, he argued, was therefore to keep the rimlands at both ends of Eurasia from falling to a single hostile power or coalition; if that happened, the United States would be encircled regardless of the size of its army and navy. The United States had gone to war twice in 30 years, he explained, because Germany and Japan had sought to dominate the Eurasian coastlands.
thinkers.now: Most of today's major flashpoints (the Black Sea, the Strait of Hormuz, India and Pakistan, the South China Sea, the Taiwan Strait, and the Korean Peninsula) lie along the rimland belt. Because the rimland is so vast, however, this alone does not prove him right. In 1942 Spykman foresaw that "a modern, vitalized, and militarized China of 400 million people" would threaten the position of the Western powers in the "Asiatic Mediterranean" (the South China Sea and the waters of Southeast Asia), and that Chinese air power might one day control that sea. The chance that China will be reported by the end of November to have again blocked resupply of Second Thomas Shoal is put at 30 percent. His prescription was to use allies in the rimland as a foothold, yet the United States, while extending its tariff truce with China to January 2027, has unilaterally scaled back its combined exercises with South Korea and imposed Section 301 tariffs on its allies. Greenland, where the United States signed a security agreement with Denmark in September, is one of the places where, Spykman wrote in 1944, the United States should base naval and air forces.
thinkers.record: In America's Strategy in World Politics (1942), he held that Germany and Japan could remain pillars of the balance of power after the war; Japan became a U.S. ally through the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty of September 1951, and West Germany through its accession to NATO in May 1955. His forecast in the same book that China, not Japan, would be the main problem in East Asia came true with the founding of the People's Republic of China in October 1949 and China's intervention in the Korean War in October 1950. The rimland logic is regarded as the geographic prototype of Cold War containment, earning him the nickname "godfather of containment." In 1944, by contrast, he judged that as long as the Soviet Union did not seek hegemony over the European rimland, it would be the most effective continental base for keeping the peace, and that cooperation among the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union would be the foundation of postwar security. That cooperation gave way to the Cold War in March 1947, when the United States proclaimed the Truman Doctrine to stop Soviet expansion.

thinkers.role: Leader of the Chinese Communist Party and founding leader of the People's Republic of China
thinkers.claim: In his lectures "On Protracted War," delivered in Yan'an in May and June 1938, he rejected both the theory that China would be subjugated and the theory that it would win quickly. Japan was strong but a small country, short of land, resources, population, and troops, and would grow increasingly isolated internationally; China was weak but a large country whose international support would grow. The war therefore had to be long, passing through three stages: the enemy's offensive and China's defense, stalemate, and China's counteroffensive. In the meantime, since the temporary and partial loss of territory was the price of holding and recovering all of it permanently, China had to avoid decisive battles and wear the enemy down through mobile and guerrilla warfare. The other pillar was the united front. "On Policy" (1940) extended to foreign affairs the principle of exploiting contradictions to win over the many, oppose the few, and crush enemies one by one, calling for Japan's allies, Germany and Italy, to be treated differently from Britain and the United States, which opposed Japan.
thinkers.now: The Russia-Ukraine war has become a war of attrition in which each side waits for the other to tire first, and the chance that a full ceasefire takes effect by the end of the year is put at 8 percent. Mao's protracted war, however, was a strategy in which the weak but large side buys time to reverse the balance of strength, a different configuration from a war of attrition in which both sides simply hold out. In the Taiwan Strait, Beijing's dual strategy (avoiding the use of force until Taiwan's presidential election in January 2028 while extracting concessions from Washington on joint-statement language and arms sales and leaning on Taiwan's opposition to influence the vote) resembles the logic of protracted war and the united front: avoid a decisive battle and make time an ally. In semiconductors, its approach of courting South Korea as a whole while singling out particular companies for pressure has the same structure as the principle of winning over the many and crushing the few one by one.
thinkers.record: His forecast to Edgar Snow on July 16, 1936, that Japan would not stop at China but would push on to the Philippines, Vietnam, the Malay Peninsula, and beyond came true with Japan's move into southern Indochina in 1941 and the outbreak of the Pacific War that December. In line with his 1938 forecast that China could not win quickly but would not be subjugated, the war dragged on for seven more years and ended with Japan's surrender in August 1945. His judgment in August 1946 that the U.S.-backed Nationalists were a paper tiger was borne out by victory in the civil war in 1949, and his decision in 1969 to make the Soviet Union the principal enemy led to U.S.-China rapprochement in February 1972. By contrast, after he set the goal in November 1957 of catching up with or surpassing Britain in 15 years, the Great Leap Forward he launched in 1958 ended in a famine in which, depending on the researcher, an estimated 15 million to 55 million people starved to death.

thinkers.claim: A Theory of Justice sought the principles people would agree to behind a "veil of ignorance," not knowing their own circumstances, talents, or values. The first principle is equal basic liberties for all; the second permits social and economic inequalities only under fair equality of opportunity and only when they are to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle). The Law of Peoples took peoples, not individuals, as its unit, and recognized as members of international society "decent" peoples that, though not liberal, do not commit aggression and respect basic human rights. "Outlaw states" that commit aggression and disregard human rights are not members. Toward "burdened societies," which lack the institutions and resources to order themselves, he set a duty of assistance that lasts until they can do so on their own, but he rejected extending the difference principle across borders. Clisa Geopolitics always identifies those who stand to lose most in its "What it means for people" section but, unlike Rawls, does not use this as the criterion for ranking.
thinkers.now: Taking individual lives as the yardstick, Clisa Geopolitics has put the return of prisoners of war and of children forcibly deported to Russia first on the agenda for ceasefire talks in the Russia-Ukraine war, and in the Russia-NATO standoff has placed the protection of civilians and safeguards against accidental clashes ahead of the Polish government's priorities. This runs close to the principle of "Fifty Years after Hiroshima" that civilians, who bear no responsibility for a war, must be distinguished from leaders and soldiers. Rawls's duty of assistance is also cited in the site's philosophy questions, but on October 9 Kim Yo Jong rejected the plan of South Korea's Ministry of Unification to provide medical equipment. Clisa Geopolitics leaves open how to distinguish a regime from its people in a system like North Korea's, where regime and state are effectively one, and this is precisely where The Law of Peoples, which takes peoples as its unit, has drawn criticism.
thinkers.record: Where he was borne out: the demand of A Theory of Justice (1971) to look first to the least advantaged became the starting point for half a century of debate over distributive and international justice. In experiments reported in 1987 by Norman Frohlich, Joe Oppenheimer, and Cheryl Eavey, groups placed in conditions modeled on the veil of ignorance were able to reach agreement, as Rawls's account predicts. Where he missed: the groups in the same experiments chose not the difference principle but a principle of maximizing average income subject to a guaranteed minimum. Buchanan pointed out that, contrary to the premise of The Law of Peoples, cross-border economic structures had already become a subject of justice. And its diagnosis, which locates the causes of poverty mainly in a society's own political culture, remains in dispute between Pogge, who stresses the responsibility of international institutions, and Joshua Cohen (2011), who stresses political culture and geography.

thinkers.role: U.S. national security adviser and secretary of state
thinkers.claim: A stable international order, he held, requires two things together. One is a balance of power in which no state can easily subjugate another; the other is legitimacy. Legitimacy here means not justice but a minimal agreement among the major powers on the shape of a workable order and on the permissible aims and methods of foreign policy. His conclusion was that once a great power rejects this agreement and seeks to overturn the order itself, balance alone cannot preserve the peace. In practice, through his secret trip to China in July 1971 and President Nixon's visit in February 1972, he built a configuration in which the United States had closer relations with both the Soviet Union and China than the two had with each other, so that the two Communist giants checked each other.
thinkers.now: The triangle he designed now stands on its head: China and Russia are closer to each other than either is to the United States. With President Trump's visit to China in May 2026 and President Xi Jinping's visit to the United States in September, the U.S.-China tariff truce has been extended to January 10, 2027, and the leaders' staging of coexistence resembles, on the surface, his proposal for a Pacific Community. By his own standard, however, the element of legitimacy, an agreement on permissible aims and methods, is missing. Semiconductor export controls were left off the agenda, and Washington has floated arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip while imposing Section 301 tariffs on its allies as well. In Ukraine, no compromise that would reach what he called "balanced dissatisfaction" is yet in sight. Russia makes the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from all of Donetsk Oblast a precondition for a ceasefire and rejects any stationing of Western troops at all.
thinkers.record: In an op-ed on March 5, 2014, he argued that Ukraine should be not an outpost of either East or West against the other but a bridge between them, and advised it not to join NATO but to adopt a posture comparable to Finland's. His warning that a contest between blocs over Ukraine was dangerous came true with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The prescription of neutrality, however, was not adopted, and he himself abandoned it after the invasion. At the World Economic Forum in Davos on May 23, 2022, he proposed a ceasefire along the prewar line, drawing protests from Ukraine, and in an essay in The Spectator that December he wrote that a peace process should link Ukraine to NATO. On January 17, 2023, he said that a neutral Ukraine no longer made sense and accepted NATO membership as an appropriate outcome. The détente of the 1970s rested on the premise that the Soviet Union would endure for a long time. At a 2007 State Department conference he recalled that Nixon and he had expected the satellite regimes of Eastern Europe to collapse, though not so quickly, and that neither Nixon nor he, nor the Soviet experts they consulted, had ever spoken of the dissolution of the Soviet Union itself.

thinkers.claim: His argument proceeds in two steps. First, China wants to be accepted as China, not as an "honorary member" of a Western order, and as a country with an ancient civilization and an enormous population it cannot help aiming to become the strongest power in Asia and, eventually, in the world. At the same time, he judged that China would not become a Western-style liberal democracy. Second, because Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and ASEAN combined cannot balance China, the United States must remain the regional balancer if the smaller countries are to have room to maneuver. He said that competition between the United States and China is inevitable but conflict is not, and warned that if the United States wants to influence Asia's strategic direction, it cannot keep going back and forth.
thinkers.now: ASEAN countries are hedging, expanding economic and diplomatic cooperation with China without cutting off security cooperation with the United States, so as to avoid lining up behind either side. By his reasoning, such hedging depends on the United States remaining the regional balancer. In 2026, however, Washington extended its tariff truce with China through summit diplomacy while floating arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip, and imposed Section 301 tariffs on its allies as well. This can be read as a sign of the vacillating United States he warned against. Since the Iran war, the countries along the Strait of Malacca have also found themselves in a harder position. In April, Indonesia's finance minister floated transit fees for the strait, then walked the idea back, and in the same month Indonesia announced an expanded military partnership with the United States. Singapore's foreign minister suggested the war in the Middle East could be a dry run for a U.S.-China war in the Pacific and voiced concern that Singapore could be caught in the middle.
thinkers.record: Start with the judgments that held up. In the 2013 interview collection he said that China would not become a liberal democracy and that if it did, it would collapse; the first part has proved right, as the Communist Party's one-party rule continues to this day. He also said China would not submit its South China Sea territorial disputes to international adjudication, and when the arbitral tribunal in The Hague constituted under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea ruled in the Philippines' favor on July 12, 2016, China rejected the award as "null and void." Some judgments missed. The merger with Malaysia that he had urged in his 1961 radio talks as Singapore's way forward, achieved in 1963, ended just two years later with Singapore's expulsion in August 1965, and the independent Singapore whose survival many doubted at the time went on to prosper. In a 2005 interview with Germany's Der Spiegel he correctly diagnosed that North Korea's leadership had staked its survival on nuclear weapons, but his forecast that the regime would eventually collapse from within has not come true more than 20 years later. In a May 2012 interview with Germany's Die Zeit he said the European Union had expanded too quickly and would probably fail, yet the EU has not broken apart, having survived even Britain's 2016 decision to leave.

thinkers.claim: In an essay in the Summer 1993 issue of Foreign Affairs, Huntington argued that the fundamental source of conflict after the Cold War would be culture rather than ideology or economics. States would remain the principal actors, but the principal conflicts would occur between nations and groups belonging to different civilizations. A civilization, in his account, is the broadest level of cultural identity, defined by history, language, tradition, and above all religion. He named the Western, Confucian, Japanese, Islamic, Hindu, Slavic-Orthodox, and Latin American civilizations and, with a qualification, an African one. His reasons included that civilizational differences form over long periods and change slowly; that growing interaction makes people more aware of those differences; that religion fills the gap left when modernization unsettles older identities; and that the West's position at the peak of its power drives non-Western societies back to their own roots. He did not deny conflict within civilizations, but he held that conflicts between them are more frequent, longer lasting, and more violent, and the most likely to escalate into global war.
thinkers.now: As of 2026, the Russia-Ukraine war has ground on as a war of attrition into its fifth year, a war between two countries that belong to the same Slavic-Orthodox civilization. The Mecca joint defense pact concluded by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan in August 2026 fits his "kin-country syndrome," in which countries of the same civilization close ranks, yet Pakistan is also fighting the Taliban regime in Afghanistan, a fellow member of the Islamic world. The 2024 treaty between North Korea and Russia is, in his classification, anti-Western cooperation linking the Confucian and Orthodox civilizations, a cross-civilizational alignment like the "Confucian-Islamic connection" he described in 1993. The relationship between North Korea and China, restored in June, amounts to solidarity within a single Confucian civilization.
thinkers.record: Some of his judgments have held up. His 1993 diagnosis that culture and religion would become the main axes of conflict once ideological rivalry ended fits a trend of great powers invoking civilization as justification, as Russia did in March 2023 when its foreign policy concept defined the country as a "state-civilization" and the center of the "Russian world." Ajami, who had criticized him in 1993, wrote in 2008 that Huntington's argument now seemed more persuasive than his own critique. Among his misses, he wrote in 1993 that violence between Ukraine and Russia was unlikely because both are Slavic and Orthodox peoples, yet the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the full-scale invasion of February 2022 followed. The 2014 uprising by armed separatists in the east partly overlapped with the split between a Catholic-leaning west and an Orthodox east that he had judged in 1996 to be more likely than war, but what Russia chose in 2022 was an all-out interstate war. As for the hypothesis that civilizational conflicts grow more frequent and more intense, Jonathan Fox analyzed data on domestic conflicts from 1945 to 2001 and reported in 2005 that conflicts between civilizations were consistently fewer than other conflicts and did not become relatively more intense after 1990.

thinkers.claim: The Grand Chessboard (1997) treated Eurasia as the central arena of global power and defined the task of the United States after the Cold War as preventing the emergence of any dominant power or coalition that could push it out of the continent. Brzezinski called countries that shape the fate of great powers by virtue of their location rather than their strength "geopolitical pivots," and he named Ukraine as the leading example. Without Ukraine, he argued, Russia cannot become a Eurasian empire; if it subordinates Ukraine again, it automatically becomes one. The most dangerous scenario, in his view, was an "antihegemonic" coalition of China, Russia, and Iran, bound not by ideology but by complementary grievances, and he expected that this time China would lead and Russia would follow. But he described it as a contingency to be averted, however remote it might be.
thinkers.now: Russia signed comprehensive strategic partnership treaties with North Korea in 2024 and with Iran in January 2025, and North Korea restored its relationship with China as well when Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited Pyongyang in June 2026. The result resembles the coalition Brzezinski warned about. Because it is bound by grievances rather than ideology, however, the limits of its cohesion show up in a crisis. With the Iran war, which began in late February 2026, still under way, the test is what China and Russia do for an Iran under a U.S. naval blockade. His proposition that Russia becomes an empire if it subordinates Ukraine again is also being tested. Russia is demanding the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from all of Donetsk Oblast as a precondition for a ceasefire.
thinkers.record: In The Grand Failure (1989), Brzezinski judged that the Soviet Union was more likely to head toward one of four outcomes than to succeed at pluralization: prolonged crisis, Brezhnev-style stagnation, a coup by the military and the KGB, or fragmentation along ethnic lines. With the attempted coup of August 1991 and the dissolution of the Soviet Union that December, two of them came to pass. His 1997 warning about an antihegemonic coalition also pointed in the right direction and took partial shape in the Russia-Iran treaty of January 2025. That treaty, however, contains no mutual defense clause, and China has signed no new alliance treaty with either country, so the China-led grand coalition he anticipated has not yet materialized. One judgment proved only half right: in The Grand Chessboard (1997) he expected Ukraine to be ready for serious negotiations with the EU and NATO sometime between 2005 and 2010. Negotiations with the EU on an association agreement began in March 2007, bearing out that forecast, but the NATO summit in Bucharest on April 3, 2008, stated only the principle of future membership and deferred a Membership Action Plan (MAP) to a later stage. Another missed the mark: events ran directly counter to his 2012 vision of bringing a reformed Russia into a "larger West," with the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the full-scale invasion in 2022. Whether the NATO and EU enlargement he supported intensified Russia's backlash remains in dispute.

thinkers.role: Harvard political scientist; former U.S. assistant secretary of defense
thinkers.claim: The Thucydides Trap is the hypothesis that when a rising power threatens to displace a ruling power, the structural stress created by the shift in power between them makes ordinary crises prone to escalate into war, even if neither side wants one. The name comes from Book 1, Chapter 23, Section 6 of the History of the Peloponnesian War, where Thucydides wrote that, contrary to the publicly stated grounds, the truest cause was that the growth of Athenian power instilled fear in Sparta and drove it to war. Allison's research team selected 16 cases over 500 years, from Portugal and Spain around the time of the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas to Britain and France versus Germany from the 1990s on, and counted 12 that ended in war (1,000 or more battle deaths per year). The team sought to collect every qualifying case rather than a sample, followed standard histories in its judgments, and relied on The New Cambridge Modern History where accounts differed. In the four cases that avoided war, Allison argues, both the challenger and the ruling power made major adjustments in their attitudes and actions.
thinkers.now: After President Donald Trump's visit to China in May 2026 and Chinese leader Xi Jinping's visit to the United States in September, the U.S.-China tariff truce was extended to January 10, 2027. This amounts to managing the relationship a few months at a time rather than the major adjustment in attitudes and actions that Allison describes; semiconductor export controls were left off the agenda, and the Chinese chipmaker CXMT's share of the DRAM market rose from 4 percent to 10 percent in a year. In the Taiwan Strait, no crisis has escalated into war since 1954, but the level of pressure has risen with each one: the effective erasure of the median line in 2022, regular Chinese coast guard patrols around Kinmen from 2024, and the announcement by China's Maritime Safety Administration of navigation controls in August 2026. What Allison warned against is a chain reaction in which such ordinary crises spread along alliance lines.
thinkers.record: In 2004, Allison wrote that on the current path, a nuclear terrorist attack on the United States within the next decade was more likely than not, but no such attack had occurred by 2014. His warning in August 2012 that structural tension between the United States and China would grow fits the course that ran from the trade war that began in 2018 to the U.S. semiconductor export controls on China in October 2022. His core claim of September 2015, however, that in light of the historical record a U.S.-China war in the coming decades is more likely than not, cannot yet be judged right or wrong because its time frame has not run out. There has been no war between the United States and China through 2026, but a lengthening period of managing tensions without war, by itself, neither confirms nor refutes the hypothesis.

thinkers.claim: Offensive realism starts from five assumptions: an anarchic system with no authority above states, the offensive capabilities of great powers, uncertainty about others' intentions, survival as the overriding goal, and states as rational actors. Because a state cannot know when another state might become an enemy, the surest guarantee of security is to be more powerful than its competitors, and great powers therefore seek to maximize their power. Global hegemony, however, is impossible because of the "stopping power of water": oceans impede the projection of military force. The realistic goal is therefore hegemony in one's own region. Mearsheimer holds that the United States, as a regional hegemon, should act as an offshore balancer, relying first on the states of other regions to keep a peer competitor from emerging there and keeping direct intervention as a last resort. By this logic, he predicted that a powerful China would seek to dominate Asia as the United States dominates the Western Hemisphere, that the United States would try to stop it, and that neighbors such as India, Japan, South Korea, and Vietnam would side with the United States.
thinkers.now: The Russia-Ukraine war continues into its fifth year. Russia makes the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from the remaining parts of Donetsk Oblast a precondition for a ceasefire and rejects any stationing of Western troops. Its demands extend beyond neutrality to territory, a cap on the size of Ukraine's armed forces, and legal recognition of the annexed lands, which sits uneasily with his 2014 prescription that a neutral buffer would suffice. The United States has asserted its dominance of the Western Hemisphere through the capture of President Nicolás Maduro in January, an energy blockade of Cuba, and a Greenland security agreement with Denmark in September, consistent with his theory that a regional hegemon first secures its primacy in its own region. By contrast, Washington's floating of arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip, its tariffs on allies, and its unilateral scaling back of combined U.S.-South Korean exercises diverge from his picture of the United States concentrating its strength on containing China, with China's neighbors lining up behind Washington.
thinkers.record: His prediction in the Chicago Tribune on January 15, 1991, that U.S. combat deaths in the Gulf War would be fewer than 1,000 proved correct. His 1993 warning that a Ukraine without nuclear weapons would be vulnerable to Russia gained weight when Ukraine, having handed its last nuclear warheads to Russia in June 1996, was invaded in 2014 and 2022. Whether nuclear weapons would have prevented the invasions, however, cannot be tested, and his 1993 expectation that Ukraine would not give up its nuclear weapons was proved wrong within three years. In 1990 he warned of instability in Europe on the premise that U.S. and Soviet forces would leave Central Europe and NATO would effectively cease to function, yet NATO grew to 32 members with Sweden's accession in March 2024. In 2014 he wrote that Putin's response was defensive rather than offensive and that Russia lacked the capability to conquer even eastern Ukraine easily; the full-scale invasion of February 2022 ran counter to the first judgment, while Russia's failure to take Kyiv that March bore out the second.

thinkers.claim: Morgenthau accepted the struggle for power as the reality of international politics, but he did not glorify power. Power, he argued, should not be an end in itself but a means to a higher purpose that gives a nation its reason for being, and its pursuit needs moral and normative limits. Universal moral principles must be filtered through concrete circumstances; without prudence, the weighing of the political consequences of seemingly moral action, there can be no political morality. He also refused to equate any one nation's moral aspirations with a universal moral law. At the end of the first edition he set out four rules of diplomacy for preserving peace (pp. 439–441): strip diplomacy of the crusading spirit; define foreign-policy objectives in terms of national security, meaning the integrity of territory and institutions, and back them with adequate power; look at the political scene from the point of view of other nations; and be willing to compromise on every issue that is not vital.
thinkers.now: Morgenthau's test is not whether force is used but whether objectives are narrowly defined in terms of vital interests, whether adequate power stands behind them, and whether room is left for compromise and retreat. Russia has made the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from the rest of Donetsk Oblast and the exclusion of Western troops preconditions for a ceasefire, placing its war aims where there is little room to negotiate. The United States, after striking Iran together with Israel on February 28, has kept up a naval blockade, and in the Western Hemisphere it has used force on several fronts: the capture of President Nicolás Maduro in January, the interception of tankers bound for Cuba and strikes on suspected drug boats. On Iran, Clisa Geopolitics ranks first a U.S. course that keeps the blockade in place while proposing a phased agreement with nuclear conditions and, if talks make no progress, falls back to a phased agreement that defers the nuclear issue to a second phase. That course narrows the objective and maps out a line of retreat in advance, in keeping with Morgenthau's rules.
thinkers.record: Start with what he got right. In an April 1965 essay in The New York Times Magazine he wrote that a guerrilla war could not be won without the active support of the population, and that because China was Vietnam's traditional enemy, Ho Chi Minh could become an Asian Tito. In 2005, John Mearsheimer wrote that Morgenthau had regarded the domino theory as nonsense. The United States left the war under the peace agreement of January 1973, Saigon fell on April 30, 1975, and China attacked Vietnam in February 1979. Vietnam, however, had signed a 25-year treaty with the Soviet Union in November 1978, just before that attack, and so did not stand outside the blocs as Tito had. Now for what he got wrong. In the first edition he judged a two-bloc system more dangerous to peace than any other balance-of-power system when the two blocs competed across the world and both were driven by the crusading zeal of a universal mission (p. 440). Yet those conditions held through the Cold War, and the United States and the Soviet Union never fought each other directly, and in 1986 John Lewis Gaddis called the postwar order the Long Peace. In a 1952 review, Alan Bullock argued that he treated Soviet diplomacy merely as a continuation of tsarist imperialism and missed its revolutionary character.
